events.title: The shore-woman's catch carried in whole
events.body: A woman of the shore households at Dùn ìseal, whose net takes more mackerel than her family can eat or smoke before it turns, carries three baskets of it to the bank herself rather than let it spoil unshared. Tormod Liath comes down from the hall to help her set them down. After it the sharing before the storms needs no one to ask.

events.title: A holder shamed into doubling his own surplus
events.body: A holder of one of the near valleys mocks a household that brings little to the sharing. His neighbours say nothing against him, but the next year he brings in double his own surplus unasked. No reciter keeps his name.

events.title: Beasag born at Àth shean
events.body: A daughter is born to a careful household at Àth shean, the ford below Dùn ìseal, some years after her father digs a grain pit under the byre floor against nothing he can name. Her mother dies bearing the last of her brothers three winters before the lean year that will end the household's place at the ford.

events.title: Lachlann born on An Cnoc Ruadh
events.body: A son is born in An Cnoc Ruadh's hall and named Lachlann, red-headed like so many of that line; he grows up wet to the knee on the lake shore and learns the salt-rake before the spear.

events.title: Oighrig born to a herder of the near slopes
events.body: A daughter is born to Dòmhnall, a herder of the near slopes above Tobar dhìreach with no kinship to Rìghrean na Cloiche, and named Oighrig; she grows up sitting her household's turns at the slab and will draw the white stone at three-and-thirty.

events.title: A lean storm season at Dùn ìseal
events.body: Failed grazing and short-headed barley along the near valleys, with three weeks lost to a wind that will not turn, make the leanest storm season since the sharing began. The division at the bank is thinner than any household remembers, and old people come to be counted though they have nothing to bring.

events.title: Beasag watches the division made by the count of mouths
events.body: Beasag, seventeen, is sent to Dùn ìseal with her household's share in the lean year and sees the sharing divided by the count of mouths: a widow with four children carries home more than she brought, and a boy holds his first full sack too long to trust it. She says nothing of her father's pit.

events.title: Beasag tells of her father's pit at the ford
events.body: In the first mild days after the storms break, a woman mending net on the bank at Àth shean asks Beasag idly whether her father's byre came through the lean year as thin as the rest. Beasag answers true: there is a pit under the floor, and he never brought it all in.

events.title: Tormod Liath sends to open the floor at Àth shean
events.body: Word of the hidden pit reaches Tormod Liath at Dùn ìseal by way of Àth shean's own holder. He asks only whether the girl told it of her own will, unbeaten and unbribed, and on being told she had, sends his men to open the floor.

events.title: The household of Àth shean put out with what it can carry
events.body: Grain enough for two households through the lean winter is found beneath the byre floor. Beasag's father is given until dark to take what his household can carry on its backs and to be off the ford's ground by morning: the first punishment under the sharing custom that is remembered.

events.title: Beasag's household settles east of the vein
events.body: After eleven days on the road, Beasag's father builds a house on a nameless slope east of the vein, where the king's blood holds no hall and claims no grazing, among households that went out a generation before for their own reasons. He digs no pit under this floor.

events.title: Sìleas Bhàn dies among her kin
events.body: Sìleas Bhàn, who opened the store within the bank by the count of mouths, dies among her own kin in the valley below the bank in her eight hundred and eightieth year; Tormod Liath comes down from the hall to stand at her burying.

events.title: Peigi born on An Cnoc Ruadh
events.body: A daughter is born to Lachlann Ruadh and named Peigi, black-haired and loud from her first night; she will meet her father's fosterling at the gate at fifteen and tell him he is too thin.

events.title: Tormod Liath dies at Dùn ìseal
events.body: Tormod Liath dies in his own hall, without wound or fever, in the three hundred and eightieth year of his holding, having outlived three heirs of his own body and buried each at the bank he built. Dùn ìseal mourns him the length of a season; scarcely a household on the hill remembers a holder before him.

events.title: Eilidh Ghlas takes up the hill
events.body: The holding of Dùn ìseal passes to Eilidh Ghlas, of the king's own blood, who has lived out those same generations in the valleys under the hill without thought of holding anything but her own hearth. She takes up the sharing custom with the hill itself, and weighs it at the bank herself in her first years.

events.title: Eilidh Ghlas asks after the pit at Àth shean
events.body: Before the bank is even swept for the season's grain, Eilidh Ghlas sends to Àth shean to ask after the pit still known by the name of the man who dug it. She is told it stands empty, and says only that this is well.

events.title: Calum Ciar stands where an heir stands
events.body: In the first sharing of his mother's own holding, Calum Ciar stands a pace behind Eilidh Ghlas's shoulder at the bank, and the ford takes notice of him for the first time. No one at Dùn ìseal afterward looks for another heir.

events.title: Eilidh weighs the old custom of the valleys
events.body: Eilidh Ghlas turns over, without acting on it, a custom she learned as a girl in the near valleys: that a household with two sons sometimes sends the younger to be raised at another hearth, so that he grows up loved rather than waiting on an inheritance not his.

events.title: The younger son born in a high river spring
events.body: A second son is born to Eilidh Ghlas at Dùn ìseal in a wet spring, when the river at Àth shean runs high enough to float the ford-stones. No reciter keeps his day, and none ever will.

events.title: A boy who does not ask to ride out
events.body: Eilidh's younger son, six years old, watches his brother ride out with the men to renew the boundary stones and does not ask to go. His mother watches him a long while from the hall door and tells her steward that a house with only one door out of it is no house for a second son.

events.title: Word sent west to An Cnoc Ruadh
events.body: Eilidh Ghlas sends word to Lachlann Ruadh, holder of An Cnoc Ruadh, asking that he take her younger son to be raised in his household. She gives it out as a mother's wish that the boy learn a trade of his own; the ford's peace is served by it besides.

events.title: Calum Ciar counts the miles at the gate
events.body: On the morning his brother leaves for An Cnoc Ruadh, Calum Ciar stands long at the gate after the party is out of sight, and tells a groom who asks him in out of the wind that he is only counting how many days fifty miles there and back will take.

events.title: Eilidh's parting at Àth shean
events.body: Eilidh Ghlas walks with her son's party as far as Àth shean and kneels to his height at the turning of the roads, telling him he is not sent for any wrong of his, that An Cnoc Ruadh will be as much home to him as Dùn ìseal, and that she means to see him grown.

events.title: A mound left untouched on Rathad an t-Salainn
events.body: On the road west, the household man Donnchadh stops before a low green mound and will go no nearer to it, telling the boy only that it is older than the road and the salt trade. A wise traveller, he is told, lets such places lie as he lets a wasp's nest lie.

events.title: Rìonach's saying of the forked river
events.body: Turning off Rathad an t-Salainn for her own kin at Àth shean, Rìonach tells the fosterling that a household not his own by birth is no loss to him but a doubling, as a forked river becomes two whole rivers rather than two lesser ones.

events.title: The fosterling comes to An Cnoc Ruadh
events.body: Eilidh Ghlas's younger son comes down to the western lake shore at evening and is met at the gate by Lachlann Ruadh and his daughter Peigi, who tells her father plainly that he is too thin and will need feeding, and carries in his one bundle herself.

events.title: Lachlann forbids the naming of a king's son
events.body: Lachlann Ruadh tells his household that the fosterling shall be called no king's son and no king's grandson, but a boy of the ford's people come to learn a trade, and warns his daughter Peigi he will hear of it if she names him otherwise again.

events.title: Calum Ciar given the boundary stones
events.body: Calum Ciar is given the judging of the near valleys' boundary stones, the first trust of its kind laid on him, and settles a dispute between two herders over a shifted marker with a plainness his mother is said to have approved of.

events.title: The fosterling first put out on the lake
events.body: The fosterling is let out on Loch chrom in a boat for the first time, and comes back to An Cnoc Ruadh wet through and pleased with himself, word of it carried east along Rathad an t-Salainn to Dùn ìseal by the carriers who walk it.

events.title: Eilidh Ghlas visits An Cnoc Ruadh
events.body: Eilidh Ghlas comes to An Cnoc Ruadh as Lachlann Ruadh's guest and sits at his own board four days, asking after the tallies and the weather as she asks after her son. Walking with her son to the western point of the lake, she tells him she will not come again for some years.

events.title: The fosterling rakes salt without breaking the crust
events.body: Lachlann Ruadh puts a salt-rake into the fosterling's hands on the drying platform above Loch chrom and shows him the turn of the wrist his own family has kept for generations. By the fourth stroke the boy lifts a clean sheet of crust whole, and Peigi Dhubh tells him it is better than she managed her own first year.

events.title: An Cnoc Ruadh list begins to call Lachlann of the fostering
events.body: In these years An Cnoc Ruadh's reciters take up the habit of naming Lachlann Ruadh also Lachlann an Altraim, Lachlann of the fostering, until in time the second name is given by the list where the first once stood, and is never afterward unsaid.

events.title: Beathag gives up the list of the slab's turns
events.body: Beathag, who has kept the household order of the slab's night watch eleven years, says at the Samhain gathering that she will keep the list no longer, after a household comes two nights running to a turn already missed. Thirty-one households now stand on it, too many for one memory to hold true.

events.title: The families agree to choose the slab's keeper by lot
events.body: At the slab's own clearing the families of Tobar dhìreach and the near valleys meet to settle the watch. An old man of the gathering proposes a single keeper chosen by lot, to hold the slab until death or infirmity, rather than turns by household. No vote is taken; the silence that follows is read as agreement.

events.title: The lot falls to Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill
events.body: At the next full dark, thirty-one households send one member each to draw from a bag of thirty pebbles and one marked white. The lot falls to Oighrig, a herder's daughter of three-and-thirty, who carries the marked stone in her belt from that night for the rest of her life.

events.title: Oighrig's father speaks of the shared name
events.body: Walking home from the drawing, Oighrig's father Dòmhnall, a herder of the near slopes with no kinship to Rìghrean na Cloiche, tells her she will spend the rest of her keeping answering travellers who mistake her for blood of Dòmhnall Clachach, the second of that name to hold the north.

events.title: Taigh na Lice raised at Tobar dhìreach
events.body: The families of the near valleys build Oighrig a house on the clearing's edge above the slab, its door set to face the stone and no other way, the first building on Dia-thìr raised for no reason but to stand near the vein.

events.title: Oighrig sits her first winter alone by the slab
events.body: Moved into the new house at the first hard frost, Oighrig finds the keeper's long unbroken watch harder than any turn shared with her own household, and begins to notice things about the stain and the stone's temper that a thousand years of turned watches had never set down.

events.title: Oighrig comes to Niocol Snaidhear with her cupped hand
events.body: In her third year of keeping, Oighrig goes to the stone-worker Niocol Snaidhear and sets her own hand on his bench, cupped as for water, asking for a cup of grey stone that will hold exactly what it holds, so that no household's handful of coal runs bigger than another's by the accident of whose palm measures it.

events.title: The first two stone cups crack in the grinding
events.body: Niocol Snaidhear loses a first cup to a hidden vein in the stone and a second to a hair-crack struck too hard near its finishing, and keeps the flawed second on his bench through the grinding of the third as a thing to learn the shape of a mistake by.

events.title: Niocol finishes the cup ground to Oighrig's hand
events.body: After eleven sittings across two summers, Niocol Snaidhear finishes a cup of grey stone fitted to Oighrig's hand, veined faintly white, holding exactly what her two cupped hands together cannot quite hold. She says the hand it copies is not her own but the hand of every hearth; Niocol begins a second cup as a copy before he is asked.

events.title: Word of the stone cup travels the near valleys
events.body: News of Oighrig's cup and the trouble it answers reaches stone-workers at three other places within the year: a woman at Àth gharbh, an old man at Achadh dhìreach, and a household at Cnoc chaol, each asking to grind a copy against it.

events.title: Oighrig carries the first cup to Àth gharbh, Achadh dhìreach and Cnoc chaol
events.body: Oighrig walks the near valleys over a year with the first cup wrapped in wool, testing each new copy against it by pouring water from one to the other on a flat stone, and sending two cups at Achadh dhìreach and one at Cnoc chaol back to the wheel when the levels do not match.

events.title: The four cups are ground true at Àth gharbh, Achadh dhìreach and Cnoc chaol
events.body: The copies of the stone cup are finished: quickest at Àth gharbh, where the worker measures against Niocol's cup throughout rather than a hand alone; slowest at Achadh dhìreach, an old man's hands steadied by his grandson through the last evenings; and, despite two false starts, fastest of all begun at Cnoc chaol.

events.title: Coinneachadh nan Cupan on the moor
events.body: At a nameless spring on the moor between Àth gharbh and Tobar dhìreach, chosen because it lies equal walking from all four places and belongs to no one household, the four keepers of the cups fill each from the same water on a flat stone and pass every cup down the line for each hand to weigh. The water stands level in all four; the place is called from that morning Coinneachadh nan Cupan.

events.title: The hills measure the coal with one measure
events.body: From the year of Coinneachadh nan Cupan, the households from the slopes above Tobar dhìreach to the poor ground of Cnoc chaol measure their handful of the vein's coal by the one cup and its three copies, and not by the hand that happens to do the measuring, a change the reciters afterward give no more than a single line.

events.title: Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill dies keeping the slab
events.body: Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill keeps the slab for the rest of her life, as the lot gave it her, and that rest is shorter than anyone at the clearing looked for: she dies in Taigh na Lice in the winter after Coinneachadh nan Cupan, and the families ask that a new lot be drawn.

events.title: The lot falls to Gilleasbuig Beag
events.body: The bag of pebbles is filled again and passed among the households near the crack. The white stone comes out in the hand of Gilleasbuig Beag, a broad, quiet man known for mending roofs and cutting hazel, who goes pale rather than glad at what his open hand shows.

events.title: A basket found under the bed-place
events.body: A kinswoman of Gilleasbuig, in his house on another errand, lifts a cloth expecting food and finds a basket of broken coal from the vein, more than any hand is owed by the handful. She says nothing that day, but tells her husband before she sleeps, and within three days the near valley knows.

events.title: Gilleasbuig does not deny it
events.body: Called to the clearing, Gilleasbuig Beag owns the basket at once and says he took the coal against a hard winter, for an old mother who sleeps cold, and for no other use. He asks, when the judgement is given, what the stone gains by the coal's return that his mother does not lose by going without it.

events.title: The families judge Gilleasbuig by silence
events.body: The households argue long in the cold before an old woman of Cnoc chaol says what none of the near families will say first: that the vein was never any one hearth's to keep behind a cloth, however true the love that took it. The clearing's silence, held past any voice rising to answer it, stands as the judgement.

events.title: Gilleasbuig Beag rowed to Eilean chrom
events.body: Three men of the near households row Gilleasbuig Beag out to Eilean chrom and put him ashore, then pull back to open water and leave him without a boat to return in. He is the first anyone remembers exiled for the vein.

events.title: A fire seen three nights on Eilean chrom
events.body: The near coast watches a small fire on Eilean chrom's low rise the first night, smaller the second, and a coal's worth of red at dusk the third, gone before full dark. No fire is seen there again, and no boat is sent to learn why.

events.title: The basket set inside Taigh na Lice
events.body: The kinswoman who found the coal carries the basket to Taigh na Lice at Tobar dhìreach and sets it under its cloth just inside the door. No household proposes burning it; it was not theirs to burn before Gilleasbuig took it, and the judgement has settled that it never will be.

events.title: The lot falls to Giorsal Bhàn
events.body: A new lot is drawn from the same bag that gave the stone to Oighrig and then to Gilleasbuig, and this time it is Giorsal Bhàn's hand that opens on the white pebble. She closes her hand on it and says she will keep it, and moves into Taigh na Lice before the month is out.

events.title: Giorsal lays the coal back under the slab
events.body: On a still morning near the year's turn, Giorsal Bhàn kneels at the slab's lower edge and presses the broken coal back into the gap between stone and earth, piece by piece, returning a second day to finish it, until the basket holds nothing at all.

events.title: "The coal went home"
events.body: By the summer after Giorsal Bhàn empties the basket into the slab's edge, the four words are already going round the near valley as if they had always been there: that the coal went home. No one near the crack can afterward say who spoke them first.

events.title: Eilean chrom left to itself
events.body: The island stands ungrazed and unfished through the years after Gilleasbuig Beag's exile. Children of the near coast are told not to ask about the island with the spring on it, and are given the same short answer when they ask anyway.

events.title: Calum Ciar comes to the clearing
events.body: Calum Ciar, elder son of Eilidh Ghlas and eleventh to hold Dùn ìseal under the king, walks up the valley to the slab and asks that the next lot be drawn at Dùn ìseal in his own sight, so the hill may see the vein's lot drawn as honestly as the hill's own.

events.title: The families refuse Calum Ciar
events.body: The households near the crack answer Calum Ciar with the same held silence they gave Gilleasbuig Beag: the lot has been drawn at the slab since the custom began and will go on being drawn there, in the sight of whoever near the crack cares to watch. Calum Ciar thanks them and does not argue it.

events.title: Calum Ciar puts the question to the king
events.body: At the ford that summer, Calum Ciar carries the same question to the king. The king hears him without anger or haste and says only that the slab is older than the hill, and older than the grove of his own crowning, and that he will not overrule so old a thing for the asking of a man not two hundred years in the world.

events.title: The line between hill and slab holds unwritten
events.body: Calum Ciar goes home from the ford and asks nothing more of it. The hill rules the grazing and calls the gatherings, answering to the king for both; the keepers rule the vein, answering to no one the telling can name. The line is sworn to in no words either side writes down, and it holds.
